claim: Neural activity underlying working memory is distributed across multiple brain regions.
source: Neural activity underlying working memory is not a local phenomenon but distributed across multiple brain regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Mnemonic internal states may emerge from inter-areal reverberation even when isolated areas cannot generate self-sustained activity.
source: We found that mnemonic internal states may emerge from inter-areal reverberation, even in a regime where none of the isolated areas is capable of generating self-sustained activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through computational modeling.

claim: The mnemonic activity pattern along the cortical hierarchy indicates a transition in space separating areas engaged in working memory from those which do not.
source: The mnemonic activity pattern along the cortical hierarchy indicates a transition in space, separating areas engaged in working memory and those which do not.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2D showing a gap in firing rates.

claim: The model predicts counterstream inhibitory bias as a mechanism for distributed working memory.
source: The model yields testable predictions, including the idea of counterstream inhibitory bias, the role of prefrontal areas in controlling distributed attractors, and the resilience of distributed activity to lesions or inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as a testable prediction in the abstract and elaborated in the Results section.

claim: Prefrontal areas play a role in controlling distributed attractors.
source: The model yields testable predictions, including the idea of counterstream inhibitory bias, the role of prefrontal areas in controlling distributed attractors, and the resilience of distributed activity to lesions or inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as a testable prediction in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7C.

claim: Distributed activity is resilient to lesions or inactivation.
source: The model yields testable predictions, including the idea of counterstream inhibitory bias, the role of prefrontal areas in controlling distributed attractors, and the resilience of distributed activity to lesions or inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as a testable prediction in the abstract and demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Working memory has been traditionally associated with mnemonic delay neural firing in localized brain areas such as frontal cortex.
source: Working memory has been traditionally associated with mnemonic delay neural firing in localized brain areas, such as those in the frontal cortex (Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster, 1973; Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Inagaki et al., 2019; Kopec et al., 2015; Romo et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Local recurrent connections and NMDA receptors are involved in the encoding of memory items in selective neural assemblies.
source: computational models uncovered the involvement of local recurrent connections and NMDA receptors in the encoding of memory items in selective neural assemblies (Amit and Brunel, 1997; Brunel and Wang, 2001; Compte et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2013; Wang, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous computational modeling work.

claim: Self-sustained neural activity during working memory has been found in multiple brain regions that often appear in coactivation.
source: self-sustained neural activity during working memory has been found in multiple brain regions; and often such highly engaged areas appear in coactivation (Christophel et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017; Leavitt et al., 2017; Sreenivasan and D'Esposito, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent experimental studies.

claim: Previous modeling efforts have been limited to exploring sustained activity in local circuits or in two interacting areas at most.
source: Previous modeling efforts have been limited to exploring either the emergence of sustained activity in local circuits, or in two interacting areas at most (Edin et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2017; Murray et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The computational model includes 30 areas distributed across all four neocortical lobes.
source: Our computational model includes 30 areas distributed across all four neocortical lobes (Figure 1A; see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inter-areal connectivity is based on quantitative connectomic data from tract-tracing studies of the macaque monkey.
source: The inter-areal connectivity is based on quantitative connectomic data from tract-tracing studies of the macaque monkey (Markov et al., 2013; Markov et al., 2014a; Markov et al., 2014b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each cortical area is modeled as a neural circuit containing two excitatory populations selective to sensory stimuli A and B, and one inhibitory population.
source: For simplicity, each of the cortical areas is modeled as a neural circuit which contains two excitatory populations (selective to sensory stimuli A and B, respectively) and one inhibitory population (Wang, 2002; Wang, 1999; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The model assumes a macroscopic gradient of outgoing and recurrent synaptic excitation.
source: In addition, the model assumes a macroscopic gradient of outgoing and recurrent synaptic excitation (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Joglekar et al., 2018; Wang, 2020), so that the level of synaptic strength is specific of each area (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of apical dendritic spines per pyramidal cells increases along the cortical hierarchy.
source: This gradient is introduced by considering that the number of apical dendritic spines, loci of excitatory synapses, per pyramidal cells increases (Elston, 2007) along the cortical hierarchy as defined by anatomical studies (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2014a; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Inter-areal long-distance outgoing projections target more strongly excitatory neurons for feedforward pathways and inhibitory neurons for feedback pathways in a graded fashion.
source: To allow for the propagation of activity from sensory to association areas, we assumed that inter-areal long-distance outgoing projections target more strongly excitatory neurons for feedforward pathways and inhibitory neurons for feedback pathways, in a graded fashion (Mejias et al., 2016; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The bias of top-down projections towards inhibitory neurons is proportional to the fraction of infragranular projections.
source: We assume that the bias of top-down projections towards inhibitory neurons is proportional to the fraction of infragranular projections (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption in the model description.

claim: A transient visual input to V1 yields activation of other visual areas such as MT during stimulus presentation.
source: In a model simulation of a visual delayed response task, a transient visual input excites a selective neural pool in the primary visual cortex (V1), which yielded activation of other visual areas such as MT during stimulus presentation (Figure 2B, upper left).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After stimulus withdrawal, neural activity persists in multiple areas across frontal, temporal and parietal lobes.
source: After stimulus withdrawal, neural activity persists in multiple areas across frontal, temporal and parietal lobes (Figure 2B, top right).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The resulting activation pattern shows substantial agreement with experimental data on which areas display WM-related activity during delay period.
source: The resulting activation pattern shows a substantial agreement with a large body of data, from decades of monkey neurophysiological experiments, reviewed in recent meta-analyses (Christophel et al., 2017; Leavitt et al., 2017), regarding which areas display WM-related activity during delay period of WM tasks (Figure 2B, bottom right).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 2B comparing model to experimental evidence.

claim: The activation pattern from the model was stimulus specific, with only the neural pool selective to the presented stimulus displaying elevated sustained activity.
source: The activation pattern from the model was stimulus specific, so only the neural pool selective to the presented stimulus in each cortical area displayed elevated sustained activity (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2C and 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Areas like 9/46d displayed a sharp binary jump of activity while areas like LIP exhibited more gradual ramping activity.
source: We observed cross-area variations of neural dynamics: while areas like 9/46d displayed a sharp binary jump of activity, areas like LIP exhibited a more gradual ramping activity.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing cross-area variations observed in the model.

claim: Population level ramping activity of LIP in the model corresponds to trial-averaged temporal accumulation of information in decision-making.
source: Such a population level, or neuron-averaged, ramping activity of LIP in our model would correspond to the trial-averaged temporal accumulation of information in decision-making (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to previous work on decision-making.

claim: Firing rates of stimulus-selective sustained activity across 30 areas revealed a separation between areas displaying sustained activity and those that did not.
source: When we plotted the firing rate of stimulus-selective sustained activity across 30 areas along the hierarchy, our results revealed a separation between the areas displaying sustained activity and those that did not (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The transition in cortical space is a novel type of abrupt transition that takes place in space rather than as a function of a network parameter.
source: This is a novel type of abrupt transition of behavior that takes place in space, rather than as a function of a network parameter like in Figure 2A.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The separation between areas appears when areas are ranked according to firing rates, anatomical hierarchy, or spine count values.
source: First, the separation between areas appears not only when areas are ranked according to their firing rates, but also when they follow their positions in the anatomical hierarchy or in the rank of spine count values (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The transition does not depend on fine tuning of parameter values.
source: Second, it does not depend on any fine tuning of parameter values.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the robustness of the transition.

claim: A simplified model consisting of a fully connected network of excitatory firing-rate nodes can demonstrate distributed WM.
source: For this reason, we developed a minimal model consisting on a fully connected network of excitatory firing-rate nodes (Figure 3A, see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The simplified network includes a linear gradient of local properties with areas at the beginning having weak self-coupling and areas at the end having strong self-coupling.
source: The network of the simplified model includes a linear gradient of local properties: areas at the beginning of such gradient have weak self-coupling, while areas at the end have strong self-coupling.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the simplified model.

claim: In the simplified model, self-excitation is too weak to generate bistability in any isolated nodes.
source: As in the more elaborated model, self-excitation is too weak to generate bistability in any isolated nodes.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the simplified model.

claim: The average network firing rate may be bistable even if local couplings are weak, as long as inter-areal connections are strong enough.
source: As this factor includes both local and global components, the average network firing rate may be bistable even if local couplings are weak, as long as the inter-areal connections are strong enough.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the mean-field analytical solution.

claim: Distributed WM patterns emerge on generic networks of excitatory units when long-range connections are strong enough and the network has a linear gradient of local couplings.
source: The simplified model demonstrates that distributed WM patterns, in which some (but not all) areas display bistability when connected to each other, may emerge on generic networks of excitatory units as long as (i) their long-range connections are strong enough and (ii) the network has a linear gradient of local couplings.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simplified model analysis.

claim: Data on area-specific number of spines per neuron monotonically increases but saturates instead of growing linearly.
source: In particular, data on the area-specific number of spines per neuron seems to monotonically increase, but saturates instead of growing linearly (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Introducing a saturating gradient makes nodes more homogeneous and prevents the network from displaying distributed WM patterns without activating all nodes.
source: Introducing this saturating gradient on the simplified model makes the nodes more homogeneous, and as a result the network is not able to display distributed WM patterns without indistinctively activating all nodes (Figure 3F, gray curve).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Assuming feedforward projections are slightly stronger while feedback projections are slightly weaker allows recovery of solutions where only a subset of areas display bistability.
source: This problem was solved when we assumed that feedforward projections (i.e. those going from lower to higher areas in the gradient) were slightly stronger while feedback projections were slightly weaker, which is consistent with the counterstream inhibitory bias hypothesis. Such assumption, needed for saturating gradients, allows to recover solutions in which only a subset of areas display bistability in the WM patterns (Figure 3F, black curve).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Introducing differences between feedforward and feedback projections is a key ingredient to achieve realistic patterns of distributed WM in a data-constrained model.
source: As indicated by the simplified model, introducing differences between feedforward and feedback projections is a key ingredient to achieve realistic patterns of distributed WM in a data-constrained model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simplified model analysis.

claim: Counterstream inhibitory bias prevents indiscriminate sustained activation across all cortical areas.
source: In the full, biologically more realistic model –which will be considered for the rest of the study –this asymmetry is introduced by considering a graded preferential targeting to inhibitory neurons by top-down projections (i.e. counterstream inhibitory bias, or CIB), which prevent indiscriminate sustained activation across all cortical areas (Leavitt et al., 2017; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For strong enough CIB, the overall firing rate of early sensory areas is reduced while activity levels of areas high in the hierarchy are maintained at appropriate values.
source: We observed that, for strong enough CIB, the overall firing rate of early sensory areas is reduced, while the activity levels of areas high in the hierarchy is maintained at appropriate values (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CIB allows distributed WM patterns to emerge for a wide range of global coupling strength.
source: This also allows distributed WM patterns to emerge for a wide range of the global coupling strength (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Moderate to strong inhibitory feedback agrees well with experimental evidence.
source: Figure 4D shows activity maps for several CIB level, revealing that a moderate to strong inhibitory feedback agrees well with the experimental evidence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D comparing model to experimental evidence.

claim: A large-scale circuit can potentially display a large number of distributed sustained activity patterns (attractors).
source: We realized that a large-scale circuit can potentially display a large number of distributed sustained activity patterns (attractors), and some of them may not be accessible by stimulation of a primary sensory area.
evidence: This is stated as a realization from the model analysis.

claim: Not all distributed attractors engage cortical areas at all lobes, and frontal areas are the ones more commonly involved.
source: Five examples of different distributed WM attractors are shown in Figure 5A, where we can appreciate that not all distributed attractors engage cortical areas at all lobes, and that frontal areas are the ones more commonly involved.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The number of attractors is an inverted-U function of the global coupling strength G, with an optimal G value maximizing the number of attractors.
source: In all four cases, the number of attractors turns out to be an inverted-U function of the global coupling strength G, with an optimal G value maximizing the number of attractors (Figure 5C, curves are normalized to have a peak height of one for visualization purposes).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the number of areas involved in a given attractor and the average firing rate of these areas.
source: Across all four cases and G values considered, we found a significant positive correlation between the number of areas involved in a given attractor and the average firing rate of these areas (Figure 5E), which constitutes an experimentally testable prediction of the distributed model of WM.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5E as a testable prediction.

claim: When the network has a high number of intrinsically multistable areas, attractors tend to only involve these areas and are largely restricted to areas at the top of the hierarchy.
source: When the network has a high number of intrinsically multistable areas (i.e. when Jmax>0.4655), attractors tend to only involve these areas and are therefore largely restricted to the areas located at the top of the hierarchy (Figure 5F, bottom left and right panels).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: When the network has zero or a low number of intrinsically multistable areas, attractors typically involve a larger number of areas and are more diverse in composition.
source: On the other hand, when the network has zero or a low number of intrinsically multistable areas (i.e. Jmax<0.4655), attractors typically involve a larger number of areas (as a larger pool of areas is needed to sustain distributed WM attractors, see top right panel in Figure 5F) and the areas involved are more diverse in their composition (Figure 5F, top left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The number of active areas in a distributed WM attractor decreases only linearly with the number of randomly inactivated areas.
source: We began by inactivating (or silencing) a given number of randomly selected areas in a visually evoked distributed WM attractor, and found that the number of active areas in the attractor decreases only linearly with the number of inactivated areas (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The activity of areas remaining in distributed WM patterns linearly decreases with the number of inactivated areas.
source: Furthermore, the activity of the areas remained in the distributed WM patterns linearly decreased their sustained activity level with the number of inactivated areas (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Silencing areas at the center of the 'bowtie hub' has a strong impact on WM.
source: Interestingly, and beyond any hierarchical dependence, the temporal and prefrontal areas that had the strongest impact are part of a subset of the anatomical network which has a very high (92%) density of connections between its nodes. This anatomical core, which has sparser connections with the remaining areas (forming the periphery of the network) is known as the anatomical 'bowtie hub' of the macaque cortex identified in anatomical studies (Markov et al., 2013; Figure 6F). Overall, silencing areas at the center of the bowtie had a deeper impact, in terms of the number of attractors surviving the silencing, than silencing areas on the periphery (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: Inactivating dlPFC (9/46d) fully prevents the emergence of distributed WM patterns evoked by external stimulation in strongly distributed WM networks.
source: For example, inactivating key prefrontal areas such as 9/46d (dlPFC) fully prevented the emergence of distributed WM patterns evoked by external stimulation (Figure 7A and b), which is in agreement with classical prefrontal lesion studies –see (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2004) for a review and a discussion of the implications for dlPFC organization.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Inactivating specific areas might lead to disinhibition of other areas and reinforcement of the attractor.
source: In some cases, inactivating specific areas might even lead to a disinhibition of other areas and to a general reinforcement of the attractor (e.g. inactivating 24c leads to a larger and faster response by area STPi, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: For networks relying on localized WM, briefly inactivating an area permanently removes the information from that area.
source: For networks relying on localized WM, areas at the top of the hierarchy maintained their selective information largely independent from each other. Consequently, briefly inactivating area 9/46d would not, for example, have an effect on the sustained activity of other areas such as 8B (Figure 7C, top row). Furthermore, the brief inactivation was enough to remove the information permanently from 9/46d, which remained in the spontaneous state after the inhibition was withdrawn.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C top row.

claim: In distributed WM networks, an area can recover encoded selective information once inhibitory pulse is removed.
source: On the other hand, silencing an area like 9/46d will slightly affect the sustained activity in other areas (such as 8B) in a network strongly relying on distributed WM (Figure 7C, middle row). However, area 9/46d will be able to recover the encoded selective information once the inhibitory pulse is removed, due to the strong interaction between cortical areas during the delay period.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C middle row.

claim: Distributed WM activity patterns can be shut down with excitatory input targeting inhibitory populations of areas high in the hierarchy.
source: We therefore explore in our model whether more spatially selective signals can shut down distributed patterns of activity. In spite of their robustness to sensory distractors as discussed above, we find that distributed WM activity patterns can be shut down with an excitatory input targeting inhibitory populations of areas high in the hierarchy.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a finding from the model.

claim: A visually evoked distributed WM attractor can be deactivated by delivering excitatory input to inhibitory populations in the top four areas of the hierarchy.
source: Figure 7C (bottom row) shows how a visually evoked distributed WM attractor is deactivated when we deliver excitatory input to the inhibitory populations in the top four areas of the hierarchy (9/46v, 9/46d, F7 and 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C bottom row.

claim: Distributed WM attractors can be controlled and deactivated by localized inhibition to a small set of frontal areas.
source: Therefore, in spite of engaging cortical areas across all four lobes, distributed WM attractors can be controlled and deactivated by localized inhibition to a small set of frontal areas.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Localized WM networks can be distracted with stimuli similar or even weaker than the minimum cue input strength required to encode a WM pattern.
source: Overall, we found that localized WM networks can be distracted with stimuli similar or even weaker than the minimum cue input strength required to encode a WM pattern, while effective distractors need to be about three times as strong in the case of distributed WM networks (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Effective distractors need to be about three times as strong in distributed WM networks compared to localized WM networks.
source: Overall, we found that localized WM networks can be distracted with stimuli similar or even weaker than the minimum cue input strength required to encode a WM pattern, while effective distractors need to be about three times as strong in the case of distributed WM networks (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The difference in distractor robustness is due to the robustness of a distributed attractor and the effect of counterstream inhibitory bias.
source: This difference is due to the robustness of a distributed attractor compared to a local circuit mechanism, but also to the effect of the counterstream inhibitory bias which dampens the propagation of distractor signals (cf. MT responses in Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text as an explanation with reference to Figure 8B and C.

claim: The model predicts a positive correlation between the number of areas involved in a WM task and their average firing rate of sustained activity.
source: First, the model predicts a positive correlation between the number of areas involved in a WM task and their average firing rate of sustained activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as an experimentally testable prediction.

claim: The model predicts that areas involved in distributed WM patterns can be briefly silenced without losing the encoded information, which will be recovered as soon as the inhibition is gone.
source: Second, our model predicts that areas involved in distributed WM patterns can be briefly silenced without losing the encoded information, which will be recovered as soon as the inhibition is gone (Figure 7, middle row), something that localized WM do not predict (Figure 7 top row; see however, related effects on continuous attractor models Seeholzer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an experimentally testable prediction with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Distributed WM is significantly more robust to distractors than localized WM.
source: Third, distributed WM is significantly more robust to distractors than localized WM (Figure 8), due to their intrinsic resilience and the inhibitory feedback condition.
evidence: This is stated as an experimentally testable prediction with reference to Figure 8.

claim: FEF areas require support from frontal areas in the form of strong excitation to maintain WM-related activity.
source: Fourth, electrophysiological recordings in macaques could test whether FEF areas require support from frontal areas (in the form of strong excitation) to maintain WM-related activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an experimentally testable prediction with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model is constrained using data from the macaque brain.
source: Given that our model is constrained using data from the macaque brain, it is interesting to discuss which of our results would extend to other conditions (and, in particular, to other animal models).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion of the model's applicability.

claim: The emergence of distributed WM requires minimal elements and is likely to emerge in cortical networks of other animals such as rodents or humans.
source: First, we have shown with the simplified model (Figure 3) that the emergence of distributed WM requires minimal elements and is therefore likely to emerge in cortical networks of other animals such as rodents or humans.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about generalizability with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The existence of CIB is a plausible condition in other species as long as the gradient of local properties grows sublinearly.
source: The existence of a CIB (Figure 4) is a requirement for distributed WM as long as the gradient of local properties grows sublinearly, which makes the CIB a plausible condition in other species as well.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about generalizability with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Graded changes of circuit properties along the cortical hierarchy provide a mechanism to explain qualitatively distinct functions of different cortical areas.
source: Theoretically, the present work is the first to show that graded changes of circuit properties along the cortical hierarchy provides a mechanism to explain qualitatively distinct functions of different cortical areas (whether engaged in working memory).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical contribution of the work.

claim: The model displays a novel form of transition across the cortex that cannot be simply explained by a parameter change laid out spatially by virtue of a macroscopic gradient.
source: Our model displays a novel form of transition across the cortex, which cannot be simply explained by a parameter change laid out spatially by virtue of a macroscopic gradient, because areas are densely connected with each other in a complex large-scale network.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical insight from the model.

claim: A few association areas should exhibit signs of dynamical criticality akin to water near a transition between gas and liquid states.
source: Such a transition implies that a few association areas should exhibit signs of dynamical criticality akin to water near a transition between gas and liquid states.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the transition phenomenon.

claim: The model uncovered a host of distinct sustained activity attractor states defined by their spatial distributed patterns in the large-scale cortical system.
source: Interestingly, the model uncovered a host of distinct sustained activity attractor states, each with its own transition location in the cortical tissue. They are defined by their spatial distributed patterns in the large-scale cortical system, independent of the number of selective neural pools per area (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Many mnemonic activity states are not produced by stimulation of primary sensory areas.
source: Many of these mnemonic activity states are not produced by stimulation of primary sensory areas.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the discovered attractor states.

claim: These attractor internal states could serve various forms of internal representations such as those not triggered by a particular sensory pathway.
source: These attractor internal states could serve various forms of internal representations such as those that are not triggered by a particular sensory pathway –or those triggered by sensory input but are encoded differently as memories (Mendoza-Halliday and Martinez-Trujillo, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the functional role of attractor states with citation.
